title: Asking questions
description: Ask yes/no questions with -aa and open questions with what, who, where, when, why, how and how much.

guide.title: Yes/no questions: add a long -aa
guide.text:
To turn any statement into a yes/no question, add a long -aa to its last word. Nothing else changes - no word order change, no 'do' or 'is'.

If the last word ends in u, the u drops: beku - ಬೇಕಾ? (bekaa?), gottu - ಗೊತ್ತಾ? (gottaa?), nimmadu - ನಿಮ್ಮದಾ? (nimmadaa?).

If it ends in e or i, a linking y appears: ide - ಇದೆಯಾ? (ideyaa?), bandide - bandideyaa? The one exception is the spoken neuter ending -utte, whose final e is simply replaced by -aa: barutte - ಬರುತ್ತಾ? (baruttaa?), hogutte - hoguttaa?

If it ends in a, the a simply lengthens: barteera - ಬರ್ತೀರಾ? (barteeraa?), illa - ಇಲ್ಲವಾ? (illavaa?) or in speech ಇಲ್ವಾ? (ilvaa?).

The answer is haudu (yes) or illa (no), or more naturally just the verb repeated: barteeraa? - barteeni.

guide.title: Question words
guide.text:
The question words mostly begin with e- or yaa-:

ಏನು (enu) what; ಯಾರು (yaaru) who; ಎಲ್ಲಿ (elli) where; ಯಾವಾಗ (yaavaaga) when; ಯಾಕೆ (yaake) why; ಹೇಗೆ (hege) how; ಎಷ್ಟು (eshtu) how much, how many; ಯಾವ (yaava) which (before a noun); ಯಾವುದು (yaavudu) which one.

The question word stays where the answer would be - usually just before the verb. It does not jump to the front as in English: neevu elli iddeera? 'you where are?'.

A sentence with a question word does not take the -aa ending.

yaake is the spoken word for 'why'; in writing you will see ಏಕೆ (eke).

examples.english: Who is he / she? Who are they?

guide.title: Question words take case endings too
guide.text:
Because question words stand in for nouns, they take the same endings as nouns:

elli (where) - ಎಲ್ಲಿಗೆ (ellige) where to; ಎಲ್ಲಿಂದ (ellinda) where from.
yaaru (who) - ಯಾರಿಗೆ (yaarige) to whom; ಯಾರನ್ನು (yaarannu) whom; ಯಾರ (yaara) whose; ಯಾರ ಜೊತೆ (yaara jote) with whom.
enu (what) - ಏನನ್ನು (enannu) what (as object, rarely needed); ಯಾವುದಕ್ಕೆ (yaavudakke) for what.
eshtu (how much) - ಎಷ್ಟಕ್ಕೆ (eshtakke) for how much; ಎಷ್ಟು ಗಂಟೆಗೆ (eshtu gantege) at what time.

A question word plus -oo gives 'any / every' words: yaaroo (anyone, no one with a negative), enoo (anything), elloo (anywhere), yaavaagaloo (always).

examples.english: Who should I give this to?

guide.title: Isn't it? and either/or
guide.text:
ಅಲ್ವಾ? (alvaa?) at the end of a sentence is the tag question 'isn't it? / right?'. It is alla + -aa; the written form is ಅಲ್ಲವಾ (allavaa) or ಅಲ್ಲವೇ (allave). It works for every person and tense.

For 'A or B?' put -aa on both choices: tee bekaa, kaafi bekaa? 'Do you want tea, or do you want coffee?'

In writing, yes/no questions often use the ending -ಏ (-e) or -ಆ (-aa) interchangeably: ಇದೆಯೇ? (ideye?) = ideyaa?

examples.english: Do you want tea or coffee?

phrases.note: Answer: gottu (yes, I do) or gottilla (no, I don't).
maadodu ('the doing') is the spoken form of maaduvudu (ಮಾಡುವುದು).
What a shopkeeper or waiter asks.
alvaa works as a tag after any statement.

phrases.english: Do you want tea or coffee?
